items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

ctx.x: Did you give him like a week’s notice this time when you left?

Yeah, I gave him proper notice this time, yeah. I played it straight this time. And after that, Benny was kind of semi-retired then. He was going to go back to New York and not do too much, so that left an opening for me to join Tommy Dorsey in 1947. And that was a great experience, a wonderful band. He had people in there like Charlie Shavers the great trumpet player, Ziggy Elman was still in the band then, Paul Smith on piano, and Tommy himself was just superb you know. I stayed with him for three years, and…

of us said “we have a chance to join Duke Ellington’s band.” So he looked at us and hesitated for about fifteen seconds, then he said “take me with you.” I’ll never forget those words you know. But he was a great man. Harry was a great player and a sensational band besides you know. But I did get a chance to work with him for a while. And then of course after that, of course with Ellington, there are so many stories about that band, and Ellington himself was an element of surprise, always. Because you never knew…

items.q: we said “we have a chance to join Duke Ellington’s band.” ... But I did get a chance to work with him for a while.

But he was a great man. Harry was a great player and a sensational band besides you know. But I did get a chance to work with him for a while. And then of course after that, of course with Ellington, there are so many stories about that band, and Ellington himself was an element of surprise, always. Because you never knew…
People talk about the difference in discipline and way to lead the band between certain guys like Benny Goodman and Ellington I guess had his own way of dealing with his personnel.

Oh yes. All those band leaders had a different way. But the great thing about Basie and Ellington, when you analyze their situation, they were both rhythm section players, piano players. And when they beat off a band, unless they were doing something in television where they had to give a down beat or something like that, but normal playing swing, they played with the rhythm for one, maybe two choruses, until that groove settled in. Then, by the time the band came in, there was no question where the time was.…

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I wrote a piece when I was in the band called Ortseam... I learned to do that from Duke’s band.

ctx.x: Did Strayhorn have a name for Duke, other than Duke?
No. I don’t think so. I think he just called him Duke. I called Duke “Maestro.”
Talk about that, how you came up with that title for Duke.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Long after I’d been with Duke and everybody, I was in New York.

ctx.x: Do you know anything about his training in Italy, how he became a musician?

He knew every aria from every opera. He studied – I was a legit performer myself. When they call me a jazz drummer, I smile, because I was brought up with the opera – all the opera [?], and classical music. Of course, Dad having a music store, I got all the records – the jazz records that came in from Louis Armstrong, Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Lionel Hampton, Cab Calloway. I knew all those records when I was a kid.
Francine said earlier that you only spoke Italian when you were a bambino. So Italian was spoken in the house?
